challenges.name: secret-scanning-quiz
challenges.title: Is this key still a problem?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the S3 upload pull request: a key that was added and removed inside the same branch, and a scanner finding on a line that reads the environment first.

questions.explanation: False. Commit a1c9e02 was pushed, so the key is on GitHub: in the branch, in refs/pull/482/head (which GitHub keeps even after the branch is deleted), in every clone and fork, and in any CI log or cache built from that commit. Squashing changes what lands on main, not what was already published. The scanner found nothing because it scanned the net diff origin/main...HEAD, where the add and the remove cancel out. The fix is to revoke the key in AWS and issue a new one, then scan every pushed commit (or block the push with push protection), not only the final diff. The misconception is that deleting a secret in a later commit, or squashing, undoes the leak; once a secret is pushed, assume it is known and rotate it.

questions.question:
Added line in src/lib/storage.ts:
+const secretAccessKey = process.env.S3_SECRET ?? "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY";

Scanner output:
src/lib/storage.ts:5 high-entropy-base64 wJal... (40 chars)

Author's reply in the review: "False positive - production sets S3_SECRET, the string is only a fallback."

Statement: "The finding is real: the literal after ?? is part of the source and the build output, and it is the key the code uses whenever S3_SECRET is unset."
questions.explanation: True. The ?? operator does not hide the string: it is committed in the repository, compiled into the bundle and shipped wherever the code runs, and it becomes the active credential in any environment that forgets S3_SECRET (a preview deploy, a new region, a local run). An entropy rule exists for exactly this case: no known prefix matched, but a 40-character base64 string with 4.66 bits per character is very unlikely to be text a person wrote. The fix is to remove the fallback and fail at startup when the variable is missing, then rotate the key. The misconception is that reading the environment first makes a hard-coded default harmless; a secret in a fallback is still a secret in the code.

challenges.name: secret-scanner-diff
challenges.title: Scan the added lines of a diff for secrets
challenges.description:
CodeDev's CI runs a "secrets" job on every pull request with the output of git diff origin/main...HEAD. Write scanDiff(diff, allowPaths), which returns the secrets found in the ADDED lines of that unified diff, and shannonEntropy(s).

Reading the diff: "diff --git" starts a file section; before its first hunk, "+++ b/<path>" names the file (drop "b/"; "+++ /dev/null" = deleted file, nothing to scan). "@@ -a,b +c,d @@" starts a hunk whose next new-file line is c (",d" may be missing); a line starting with "@@" without that shape ends the hunk. Inside a hunk, "+" is an added line (it gets the current number, then the number goes up by 1), " " or an empty line is context (number + 1), "-" (removed) and "\" (No newline at end of file) do not change the number. "+++" and "---" inside a hunk are added and removed lines, not headers. Ignore a trailing "\r".

Skip files whose path starts with one of allowPaths and added lines containing the marker codedev-scan:allow. Pattern rules, on the text after "+", each at most one finding per line (its first match): aws-access-key-id (AKIA or ASIA + 16 of A-Z 0-9, no letter or digit just before or after), github-token (gh[pousr]_ + 36 or more of A-Z a-z 0-9, or github_pat_ + 22 or more of A-Z a-z 0-9 _, no letter, digit or _ just before), slack-token (xox[baprs]- + 10 or more of A-Z a-z 0-9 -, no letter or digit just before), private-key (-----BEGIN, zero or more words of A-Z 0-9, PRIVATE KEY-----), generic-secret (a name of A-Z a-z 0-9 _ ending in key, token, secret or password in any case and not preceded by A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . -, an optional quote, optional spaces, ":" or "=", optional spaces, an optional quote, then a value of 8 or more of A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - + / = . that does not start with "process.env.").

Entropy, only when no pattern rule matched the line: take the "..." and '...' literals from left to right (not backticks); a literal is a candidate when it has 20 or more characters, all of A-Z a-z 0-9 + / = _ -. All hex (0-9 a-f A-F): high-entropy-hex when H >= 3.0; otherwise high-entropy-base64 when H >= 4.5, with H = -sum(p * log2 p) over distinct characters. Report only the first candidate that passes.

Each finding is { file, line, rule, preview } with line = number in the new file and preview = first 4 characters of the secret + "... (" + length + " chars)" (the secret is the whole match, the value for generic-secret, the literal's content for entropy). Sort by file, line, then rule in plain string order. The runner reads { diff, allowPaths } and prints the array as JSON. The full rules are also in the comment at the top of the starter; every secret in the tests is fake.
hints: Before any regex: which number does each added line have in the new file, and which kinds of diff lines move that number? If your line numbers are right for a diff without secrets, the rules are the easy part.

Look at the state you carry from one line to the next (current file or none, inside a hunk or not, next new-file line number), then at the order of the checks for one added line: allowed path, marker, the five pattern rules, and the entropy check only when no pattern matched. The sort happens once, at the end.

A similar trace on other input: the hunk "@@ -7,3 +7,4 @@" followed by " a", "-b", "+c", " d", "+e" gives a = line 7, c = line 8 (b moved nothing), d = line 9, e = line 10. For entropy, "aabb" has two characters with p = 0.5 each, so H = 1.0, and "abcd" has H = 2.0: twenty characters can never exceed log2(20) = 4.32 bits, which is why a 20-character base64 string cannot reach 4.5.
